blocks.content: Open a chat and messages land instantly, in both directions. Two people edit the same Figma file and see each other cursors move in real time. A multiplayer game keeps every player in sync many times a second.
All of these need something normal web requests cannot give: a connection that stays open, where the client and the server can both send a message at any moment. That is exactly what a WebSocket is.
The web quietly runs on these connections. The green presence dots, the live cursors, and the instant message delivery you take for granted are almost all WebSockets underneath.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278418218-547998914.png
blocks.alt: WebSockets: one persistent two way connection between client and server

blocks.content: 1. What WebSockets Are

A WebSocket is a single, long lived connection between a client and a server that allows full two way communication. Once it is open, either side can send data to the other at any time, with almost no overhead per message.
It is often described as full duplex, which simply means both directions are open at once, like a phone call rather than walkie talkies where only one person can speak at a time.

["Persistent: the connection stays open instead of closing after each message","Two way: the server can push to the client without being asked","Low overhead: after the setup, each message carries only a few bytes of framing","Low latency: no new connection or headers per message"]
items: Persistent: the connection stays open instead of closing after each message
Two way: the server can push to the client without being asked
Low overhead: after the setup, each message carries only a few bytes of framing
Low latency: no new connection or headers per message

blocks.content: The mental model is a phone call, not a letter. With HTTP you post a letter and wait for a reply, and every letter is separate. With a WebSocket the line stays open, so either side can just talk whenever it wants.
That single idea, a line that stays open both ways, is what unlocks everything else on this page.
2. Why WebSockets Exist
To see why they were needed, look at what came before. Normal HTTP is request and response: the client asks, the server answers, and the connection is done. The server can never speak first.

People faked real time on top of that with polling. Short polling asks again and again on a timer and wastes most requests. Long polling holds a request open until data is ready, which is better but still opens a fresh request for every single message.

WebSockets remove the workaround entirely. Instead of many short requests, there is one connection that stays open, so a message in either direction is just a few bytes down a pipe that is already there.

Concretely, a chat on plain HTTP might poll every two seconds and still feel laggy, while the same chat on a WebSocket delivers each message the instant it is sent, using a small fraction of the traffic.

blocks.title: The key shift
blocks.content: HTTP was built for the client to pull. WebSockets give you a true push channel, so the server can send the instant something happens without the client asking.
3. The Handshake: From HTTP to a Socket
blocks.text: 3. The Handshake: From HTTP to a Socket

blocks.content: A WebSocket does not start as its own protocol. It begins as an ordinary HTTP request that asks to upgrade the connection, and only after the server agrees does it switch to the WebSocket protocol on the very same connection.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278420228-457776884.png
blocks.alt: The handshake: an HTTP upgrade request answered with 101, then the socket opens

blocks.content: The client sends a normal looking request with a couple of special headers.

GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
blocks.code:
GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

codes.http:
GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

blocks.content: If the server supports WebSockets, it replies with status 101 Switching Protocols. From that point the HTTP part is over, the connection stays open, and both sides speak the WebSocket protocol.
This is why WebSockets work through most firewalls and proxies. They start life on ports 80 and 443 as normal web traffic, and the secure form is wss, which runs over TLS just like https.

In its reply the server also echoes a computed Sec-WebSocket-Accept value, derived from the client key. This proves the server truly understood the WebSocket handshake and is not just a plain HTTP server answering by accident.
4. The Connection Lifecycle
A WebSocket connection moves through a small set of states, and understanding them makes the code and the failures much clearer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028314-452856243.png
blocks.alt: The lifecycle: connecting, open, closing, closed

blocks.content: ["Connecting: the handshake is in progress","Open: the connection is live and both sides can send messages freely","Closing: one side has sent a close frame and the other is acknowledging","Closed: the connection is fully shut down"]
items: Connecting: the handshake is in progress
Open: the connection is live and both sides can send messages freely
Closing: one side has sent a close frame and the other is acknowledging
Closed: the connection is fully shut down

blocks.content: When a side closes, it sends a close frame with a numeric code and a reason, such as 1000 for a normal close or 1006 when the connection dropped abnormally. Those codes help the client decide whether to reconnect.

While a connection is open, both sides also exchange small ping and pong control frames. These are heartbeats that prove the other end is still there, which matters because a dropped connection does not always announce itself.
5. Messages and Frames
Data on a WebSocket travels in frames. A single message can be split across several frames, and the protocol reassembles them, so from your code you simply send and receive whole messages.

["Text frames carry UTF-8 text, usually JSON in practice","Binary frames carry raw bytes, useful for images, audio, or compact formats","Control frames handle ping, pong, and close, and are never seen by your app logic"]
items: Text frames carry UTF-8 text, usually JSON in practice
Binary frames carry raw bytes, useful for images, audio, or compact formats
Control frames handle ping, pong, and close, and are never seen by your app logic

blocks.content: Because the framing is tiny, sending a message over an open WebSocket costs far less than an HTTP request, which must carry a full set of headers every time. That is a big reason WebSockets feel so fast for chatty workloads.

One thing WebSockets do not give you is routing. The protocol just delivers raw messages, so your application defines the message format, usually a small JSON object with a type field, and decides who should receive each one.
Most apps use text frames with JSON because it is easy to debug. Binary frames matter when you need compactness or speed, such as streaming audio, game state, or a custom protocol.
There is no fixed limit on message size in the protocol, but sending very large messages over a socket can block other messages, so big payloads are usually chunked or sent as binary.
6. Client and Server in Code
On the browser, the WebSocket API is built in and small. You open a connection, then react to open, message, and close events.
On the server, a library handles the handshake and gives you a socket per client. Here is a tiny broadcast server using the Node ws library, which relays every message to all connected clients.
That handful of lines is a working real time chat backend. The same idea, with rooms and authentication added, is what powers production messaging systems.

This naive broadcast loops over every connected client, which is fine on one server. Across many servers you would instead publish the message to a broker, and each server would deliver it to its own clients, which is the scaling pattern shown later.
7. A Real Example: A Chat Room
blocks.text: 7. A Real Example: A Chat Room

blocks.content: Let us make it concrete with a group chat room, the classic WebSocket use case.

["A user opens the chat, and the browser opens a WebSocket to the server with an auth token","The server checks the token, accepts the socket, and adds it to the room named general","When anyone sends a message, the server receives one frame and broadcasts it to every socket in that room","Each member sees the message appear instantly, with no request of their own","Typing indicators and read receipts travel the same way, as tiny messages over the open sockets"]
items: A user opens the chat, and the browser opens a WebSocket to the server with an auth token
The server checks the token, accepts the socket, and adds it to the room named general
When anyone sends a message, the server receives one frame and broadcasts it to every socket in that room
Each member sees the message appear instantly, with no request of their own
Typing indicators and read receipts travel the same way, as tiny messages over the open sockets

blocks.content: Notice there is no polling anywhere. The moment one person sends, everyone else receives, because every member is already holding an open connection to the server.

blocks.title: Rooms and channels
blocks.content: Servers group sockets into rooms or channels so a message reaches only the right people. A broadcast to a room of 50 is 50 sends, not a message to every user on the whole platform.
8. WebSockets vs HTTP, Long Polling, and SSE
blocks.text: 8. WebSockets vs HTTP, Long Polling, and SSE

blocks.content: WebSockets are one option among several. Seeing them side by side makes the tradeoffs clear.

{"headers":["Aspect","HTTP request","Long polling","SSE","WebSockets"],"rows":[["Direction","Client to server","Client to server, held","Server to client","Two way"],["Connection","New per request","Reopened each time","One long lived","One persistent"],["Latency","Request bound","Near real time","Real time","Real time, lowest"],["Overhead per message","Full HTTP headers","Full HTTP headers","Small","Very small"],["Best for","Normal APIs","Simple near real time","Live feeds","Chat, games, collaboration"]]}
The short version: if data flows only from the server, SSE is simpler. If both sides talk constantly, WebSockets win. If you cannot run a socket server at all, long polling is the fallback.
There is also an operational difference. HTTP requests are easy to cache, log, and debug with standard tools, while a long lived WebSocket needs its own monitoring, which is a real cost to weigh.
9. When to Use WebSockets
WebSockets are the right tool when communication is genuinely two way and frequent, and low latency matters.

["Chat and messaging, like WhatsApp web and Slack","Collaborative editing, like Figma and Google Docs, where many cursors update live","Multiplayer games, where state syncs many times a second","Live trading and betting, where both quotes and orders flow","Live dashboards where the user also sends commands"]
items: Chat and messaging, like WhatsApp web and Slack
Collaborative editing, like Figma and Google Docs, where many cursors update live
Multiplayer games, where state syncs many times a second
Live trading and betting, where both quotes and orders flow
Live dashboards where the user also sends commands

blocks.content: It is just as important to know when not to use them:

["Data flows only from the server, where SSE is simpler","Updates are rare, where occasional polling is fine","You cannot run or scale a stateful connection fleet","A strict network blocks the upgrade, where long polling still gets through"]
items: Data flows only from the server, where SSE is simpler
Updates are rare, where occasional polling is fine
You cannot run or scale a stateful connection fleet
A strict network blocks the upgrade, where long polling still gets through

blocks.content: They are overkill when data flows one way or updates are rare. A notifications feed or a stock ticker that only streams down is a better fit for SSE, and an occasional status check is fine with simple polling.
Reach for WebSockets when the client and server both need to speak often and instantly. If only the server speaks, prefer SSE.
10. Scaling WebSockets

This is where WebSockets get hard, and where interviews focus. Unlike a stateless HTTP request that any server can handle, a WebSocket is stateful. Each client is pinned to one specific server for the whole life of the connection.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028626-914678346.png
blocks.alt: Scaling: sticky sessions pin clients, a broker fans events to all servers

blocks.content: Two problems follow. First, a normal load balancer that spreads requests around will break a connection, so you need sticky sessions or a connection aware balancer. Second, when an event happens on one server, the users who need it may be connected to a different server.

["Pin connections with sticky sessions so a client stays on its server","Fan out through a broker: publish each event to Redis or Kafka, which delivers it to every server so each pushes to its own clients","Mind the connection limits, since each open socket costs memory, which is the classic problem of holding hundreds of thousands of connections per machine","Use a managed layer, like a WebSocket gateway or a service such as Pusher or Ably, when you do not want to run the fleet yourself"]
items: Pin connections with sticky sessions so a client stays on its server
Fan out through a broker: publish each event to Redis or Kafka, which delivers it to every server so each pushes to its own clients
Mind the connection limits, since each open socket costs memory, which is the classic problem of holding hundreds of thousands of connections per machine
Use a managed layer, like a WebSocket gateway or a service such as Pusher or Ably, when you do not want to run the fleet yourself

blocks.content: Deploys need care too. Restarting a server drops every connection it holds, so production systems drain connections gracefully and rely on the clients automatic reconnection to spread back across the fleet.
11. Reliability: Heartbeats, Reconnection, Backpressure
A long lived connection will eventually drop. Wi Fi changes, laptops sleep, and proxies time out idle connections. A good WebSocket client plans for this instead of assuming the pipe is always there.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278425370-535184366.png
blocks.alt: Heartbeats catch a dead connection, and the client reconnects with backoff

blocks.content: ["Heartbeats: send periodic ping and pong so a silently dead connection is detected quickly","Reconnection: on close, reconnect automatically, with exponential backoff so a mass outage does not stampede the server","Resume: track the last message id so after reconnecting you can fetch anything missed during the gap","Backpressure: if the server pushes faster than a slow client can read, buffer or drop, or the memory will grow without bound"]
items: Heartbeats: send periodic ping and pong so a silently dead connection is detected quickly
Reconnection: on close, reconnect automatically, with exponential backoff so a mass outage does not stampede the server
Resume: track the last message id so after reconnecting you can fetch anything missed during the gap
Backpressure: if the server pushes faster than a slow client can read, buffer or drop, or the memory will grow without bound

blocks.content: A good rule is to make the client the resilient side. Assume the connection will drop, and design the client to reconnect, resume, and keep working, rather than trusting that the socket is always healthy.

blocks.title: The silent failure
blocks.content: Without heartbeats, a broken connection can look open for minutes. The socket only errors when you try to send, so both sides ping to fail fast and reconnect.
12. Security
A persistent connection still needs the same care as any endpoint, and a few things are easy to miss because the usual per request checks do not repeat on every message.

["Use wss, the TLS encrypted form, exactly as you use https","Authenticate at the handshake, usually with a token, since there is no per message login","Check the Origin header to block cross site connection hijacking","Re verify authorization for sensitive actions, because a connection can stay open long after a token expires","Rate limit messages per connection so one client cannot flood the server"]
items: Use wss, the TLS encrypted form, exactly as you use https
Authenticate at the handshake, usually with a token, since there is no per message login
Check the Origin header to block cross site connection hijacking
Re verify authorization for sensitive actions, because a connection can stay open long after a token expires
Rate limit messages per connection so one client cannot flood the server

blocks.content: Be careful how you pass tokens. A token in the URL can leak into logs and proxies, so prefer sending it in an initial message or a subprotocol, or use a short lived ticket fetched over https just before connecting.
Treat every incoming message as untrusted input and validate it, exactly as you would validate the body of an HTTP request.
13. Common Mistakes

["Using WebSockets when data only flows one way, where SSE is simpler","Load balancing connections like stateless requests, which drops them","Forgetting heartbeats, so dead connections linger and updates silently stop","No reconnect or backoff, so a blip becomes a stampede when everyone retries at once","Ignoring backpressure, letting a slow client balloon server memory","Trusting the client, skipping auth at the handshake or per action checks"]
items: Using WebSockets when data only flows one way, where SSE is simpler
Load balancing connections like stateless requests, which drops them
Forgetting heartbeats, so dead connections linger and updates silently stop
No reconnect or backoff, so a blip becomes a stampede when everyone retries at once
Ignoring backpressure, letting a slow client balloon server memory
Trusting the client, skipping auth at the handshake or per action checks

blocks.content: 14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When a design needs live, two way updates, WebSockets are the answer, but the interviewer is really testing whether you understand the stateful cost.
Justify the choice: I use WebSockets when both sides send frequently, like chat or collaboration, and I would use SSE if data only flowed from the server.
Explain the handshake: It starts as an HTTP upgrade that the server answers with 101, then the same connection becomes a full two way socket.
Lead with scaling: Connections are stateful, so I add sticky sessions and a Redis pub sub layer to fan events across servers, and I watch per server connection limits.
Show reliability thinking: I add heartbeats to detect dead connections, reconnect with backoff, and resume from a last message id so nothing is lost.
